newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kinshasa fears bloodbath after talks cancelled.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa fears bloodbath after talks cancelled.

text.p: The word "bloodbath" was on many lips on Thursday as the residents of Kinshasa braced for a possible imminent battle for Zaire's capital.

Commentators in the city not only fear the battle with advancing rebels but also the government army spiralling out of control in the city of five million, the last bastion of the 32-year-old government of President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"We're heading directly for a bloodbath. It's a question of balance of forces. Kabila knows he has the upper hand," said Mobutu aide Kabuya Lumuna.

The peace process brokered by South Africa and the United Nations limped on, following Wednesday's abrupt cancellation of a "last-ditch" meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who is demanding that Mobutu quit power.
"They want the head of state to leave but we cannot agree how to do it," the Mobutu aide told Reuters.
The on-again, off-again dialogue seeking a non-violent transition of power in Zaire was increasingly discounted in Kinshasa.
Opposition politician Mukendi wa Mulumba said: "There was nothing to expect from this meeting. We couldn't expect Mobutu to resign. He's so proud of himself, he hasn't changed, he's not sincere."
"Confrontation is inevitable. We will have two or three bad days from now on," he told Reuters.
The government maintains that rebel forces are being held up by the army some 200 km (120 miles) east of Kinshasa, but the rebels say they are much closer to the city.
The opposition newspaper La Reference Plus said that with the face-to-face talks off for now, "the military option has every chance of triumphing".
"Failing a check on the Zaire armed forces, Kinshasa will assuredly become the theatre for a military clash which will be fatal as much for its people as for its infrastructure."

Although it was Mobutu who showed up for the talks and Kabila who failed to appear, the paper condemned Mobutu for behaving in an "overly suicidal" manner by refusing to simply step down and thereby spare the capital.
"Big dictators only negotiate their departure on the basis of a bloodbath," the editorial concluded.

Across the river in Brazzaville, capital of Congo, U.S., British, French, Belgian and Portuguese troops were waiting with helicopters and fast boats to pluck foreign nationals to safety should Kinshasa become a battleground.
